analysis.one_liner: Expands the child tax credit, adds paid parental leave through Social Security, and funds anti-abortion pregnancy centers.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one House Republican with zero cosponsors and referred to five committees, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the child tax credit to $3,500 per child ($4,500 for children under six), make the adoption tax credit refundable, let parents draw up to three months of paid leave from Social Security (repaid later out of their retirement checks), and extend WIC coverage for new mothers from one year to two. It would also steer new grants to pregnancy resource centers and mentoring programs that do not provide abortions, bar abortion providers from those funds, and require public colleges to tell pregnant students about resources that exclude abortion. None of it happened: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Working and middle-income families with children would get a larger child tax credit — $3,500 per child, $4,500 for a child under six, with the higher income phase-out threshold made permanent — plus a refundable adoption credit [S2][S3]. New parents could take up to three months of paid parental leave paid through Social Security [S2][S3]. New mothers would stay eligible for WIC for two years after giving birth instead of one [S2]. Mothers could require biological fathers to pay at least 50% of out-of-pocket pregnancy and delivery medical costs [S2]. Pregnant college students would be entitled to information about their rights and accommodations at public universities [S2][S3]. Unemployed noncustodial parents behind on child support would be first in line for $100 million in job-training grants [S3]. Pregnancy resource centers, maternal mentoring programs, and religious social-service organizations would gain new federal funding and legal protections [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families with children; pregnancy centers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit to $3,500 per child and $4,500 for children under six, keeps the phase-out threshold at $400,000 for joint filers, and raises the refundable portion to 15.3% of earned income.
Creates up to three months of paid parental leave for birth or adoption, paid through Social Security at a rate based on the parent's projected retirement benefit, with applications available online.
Makes the adoption tax credit refundable, so families who adopt can receive the full credit even if they owe little tax.

Extends WIC postpartum eligibility from one year to two, and requires states to make biological fathers pay at least half of a mother's out-of-pocket pregnancy and delivery medical costs at her request.
Requires public colleges to annually inform students of pregnant students' rights and accommodations under Title IX and to report to Congress on pregnancy-related complaints.
Transfers $100 million from an existing welfare contingency fund for job-training grants aimed at noncustodial parents who are unemployed or behind on child support.

Authorizes $100 million a year for community-based maternal mentoring programs and grants for pregnancy resource centers that do not provide abortions, plus a federal 'life.gov' website listing pregnancy resources.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the larger child tax credit and new grant programs, offset in part by eliminating the federal deduction for state and local taxes — a change that falls hardest on itemizers, concentrated in higher-income households in high-tax states [S2][S3]. Parents who take the paid leave would repay its full cost later, through reduced retirement checks (up to the first 60 monthly payments) or a later retirement age [S3]. Public colleges would take on new information and annual reporting duties [S3]. Abortion providers would be barred from the bill's new grants, resource lists, and mentoring funds as 'prohibited entities' [S3].

drawbacks.text: The paid leave is not free: parents must repay the full cost of the benefit through deductions from their own future Social Security retirement checks or by accepting a later retirement age, making it an advance on their retirement rather than new money.

The refundable child credit is tied to earned income and requires a qualifying Social Security number for the child, so families with no earnings and some immigrant families would get little or nothing — unlike the fully refundable 2021 credit this bill would replace.
The bill makes cooperating with state child-support agencies a condition of SNAP food assistance, meaning a parent who does not cooperate could lose food benefits.

The new funding and the life.gov resource website exclude any entity that performs, refers for, or counsels in favor of abortion, steering public money toward anti-abortion pregnancy centers and requiring the site to emphasize 'alternatives to abortion' and 'abortion risks' while excluding abortion services.

The religious-organizations section guarantees faith-based providers federal social-service funds while preserving their exemptions from nondiscrimination employment laws, limiting audits to segregated accounts, and preempting contrary state and local rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core family benefits are real and sizable: a $3,500–$4,500 child credit, refundable adoption help, extended WIC, and three months of paid leave would materially help working parents, and the SALT repeal that helps pay for it falls mostly on higher-income itemizers. But the design carries strings an honest supporter should acknowledge: the paid leave is repaid out of the parent's own future retirement benefits, the credit skips families with no earnings, food aid becomes conditional on child-support cooperation, and the pregnancy-related funding streams are built to exclude abortion providers and channel money to religious and anti-abortion counseling organizations.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in five House committees from September 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, never receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Ashley Hinson introduced the bill on September 15, 2022, and it was referred the same day to five committees — Ways and Means, Agriculture, Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary — with jurisdiction to be determined later by the Speaker.

Over the following seven weeks it was referred to three subcommittees: Health (September 16), Nutrition, Oversight, and Department Operations (October 4), and the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties (November 1).
No hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed, and no other member signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's entire life.
The bill died automatically when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, leaving its family-benefit and anti-abortion provisions unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, nothing changed: families received no new benefits, and the smaller post-2021 child credit, SNAP rules, and current funding for abortion providers all stayed as they were. Those better off are the bill's likely opponents — abortion providers and supporters of the existing tax and food-assistance rules — plus high earners in high-tax states who kept their SALT deduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; opponents of its abortion restrictions

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken to measure partisan split: a Republican introduced it with zero cosponsors, and the Democratic chairs of all five referred committees let it sit without action.

industries.note: The bill directs federal grants and the new life.gov resource listing to centers that do not provide abortions, while barring entities that perform, refer for, or counsel in favor of abortion. For pregnant women seeking material help these centers offer free services; for women considering abortion the funding is designed to steer them away from that option.

As 'prohibited entities,' abortion providers would be excluded from the bill's mentoring grants, pregnancy-center grants, and life.gov resource lists, and college resources must exclude abortion services. The bill would cut them out of new public funding streams while routing equivalent support to competitors.

The bill guarantees religious organizations equal access to federal social-service funding, lets them keep religious hiring exemptions, limits audits to segregated federal accounts, and preempts contrary state laws. That locks faith-based providers into federal social services while they retain the right to hire on religious grounds.

Repealing the federal deduction for state and local taxes raises revenue mostly from higher-income households in states with high taxes, and the bill uses that revenue to help pay for the expanded child credit. Their loss funds benefits for working families.

Institutions would face new mandates: annual pregnancy-rights information campaigns that exclude abortion services, student surveys, and reports to Congress on pregnancy-related complaints. The compliance burden is real but modest, and the information would go to students.
